opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. This is really the core question behind a lot of what we do in developmental interpretability and singular learning theory.

Start with the basic puzzle. Two networks can reach the same low training loss and agree on every training example, yet one has memorized a lookup table and the other has learned something like the actual algorithm. Looking only at the loss value, they're indistinguishable. So you need a signal beyond "how well does this fit the data."

Geometry gives you that signal. The classical intuition is flat versus sharp minima: solutions in broad basins tend to generalize better. That intuition is roughly right, but it's too crude. Measures like the Hessian assume the minimum is a nice quadratic bowl, and in neural networks it almost never is. These models are what we call singular. There are huge degenerate directions where you can move parameters without changing the function at all, and the loss surface near a solution can have a complicated, non-quadratic structure.

Singular learning theory replaces "flatness" with a better-founded quantity, the local learning coefficient, or LLC. Roughly, it measures how much of parameter space near a solution achieves close to the same loss, and how that volume scales as you tighten the tolerance. A lower LLC means a more degenerate solution: one that uses fewer effective degrees of freedom. You can think of it as a principled, geometric measure of model complexity, and it appears directly in the asymptotics of the Bayesian free energy and generalization error.

Here's why that matters for your question. A memorizing solution typically has to pin down many parameters precisely to store all those specific input-output pairs, so it tends to have a higher LLC. A solution that implements a compact, general algorithm leaves more directions free, because the mechanism is simpler and more structured, so it tends to have a lower LLC. Two solutions with the same training loss can differ in this geometric complexity, and that difference relates to how they'll behave off-distribution.

What makes this practical is that the LLC can now be estimated at scale using stochastic-gradient MCMC methods. We can track it over training and watch it change. In toy settings like modular arithmetic, you can see grokking-style transitions show up in the geometry, as the model moves from a memorization regime toward a more structured solution. In transformers, we've seen distinct developmental stages appear as plateaus and shifts in the LLC, lining up with the formation of things like induction heads.

The most exciting direction, I think, is going beyond a single scalar. We're working on refined and weight-restricted versions of the LLC that measure degeneracy for particular components or particular data distributions. Then you can ask more pointed questions. Is this attention head's contribution simpler on this subset of data? Did this circuit form general structure or task-specific structure? That moves us toward actually reading out which algorithm a network has learned from its geometry.

I should be honest about the caveats. The theory is cleanest in idealized Bayesian settings, and SGD isn't exactly Bayesian inference. The LLC estimates are sensitive to hyperparameters, and we're still building the empirical track record. But the overall picture is that the loss landscape stores information about the structure of the solution that training loss alone throws away. If we want to tell apart models that look identical on the data we have, geometry is one of the most promising places to look.

r001.rationale: The response says models with the same training loss can differ in geometric complexity, and that this difference helps distinguish their behavior off-distribution.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the core bet behind a lot of what we're doing with singular learning theory, and I think the framing you just gave is exactly right. The problem is that the training loss, by itself, is kind of a lie of omission. You can have two networks, or two regions of parameter space, that sit at essentially the same loss on your training data, and they are implementing completely different algorithms underneath. One of them might have genuinely learned the rule, and the other has memorized a lookup table, or found some shortcut heuristic that happens to work on your distribution. And if all you look at is the value of the loss, you literally cannot tell them apart.

What geometry gives you is a way to ask a different question: not "how low is the loss here," but "what does the loss look like in the neighborhood around here." And the key insight from Watanabe's work, from singular learning theory, is that for neural networks these neighborhoods are really weird. The classical picture you learn in a stats class is that around a minimum, the loss is a nice quadratic bowl, and you can count effective parameters by counting the directions where the bowl curves up. But neural networks are singular models, the Hessian is degenerate almost everywhere, and so those bowls are more like valleys and ravines and these strange higher-order shapes where the loss stays flat along some directions and curves very sharply along others.

The quantity we care about is what Watanabe calls the real log canonical threshold, which we usually just call the learning coefficient, or lambda. You can think of it as the right generalization of "effective parameter count" to the singular setting. It measures, roughly, how quickly the volume of parameter space with loss below some threshold shrinks as you lower that threshold. A simple solution, in the sense of one that's implemented by a low-dimensional, highly degenerate region, has a small lambda. A complex solution that depends delicately on many parameters has a large lambda.

And here's the connection to generalization: the Bayesian free energy, which is what actually controls the posterior and in turn what the network will tend to generalize as, has this expansion where the loss term is the leading piece, but the next term is lambda times log n. So two solutions with the same training loss get differentiated by lambda. The lower-complexity one is favored, and it's favored more strongly as you accumulate more data. That's the mechanism by which the geometry breaks the tie that the loss alone can't.

Concretely, what we do is estimate this learning coefficient locally. We take a trained model, we run a sampler, typically SGLD, in the vicinity of the current weights, and we measure how the loss behaves as you perturb around that point. That gives you the local learning coefficient. And what's been really striking in the experiments is that this number tracks things that the loss doesn't. In the toy models of superposition work we did with Dan Murfet and others, you see the local learning coefficient change in these discrete steps during training that correspond to the network moving between qualitatively different solutions, different geometric arrangements of features. The loss curve is smooth and boring, and the learning coefficient is telling you that the algorithm just changed.

The grokking setting is maybe the cleanest illustration of the thing you're asking about. You've got a network that's hit zero training loss on modular arithmetic, and it's memorizing. Then, much later, it generalizes, and the training loss barely moves during that transition. But the geometry does move. The memorizing solution and the generalizing solution live in different parts of the landscape with different degeneracy structure, and you can see the network traverse from one to the other even though the thing you'd normally be plotting is flat.

So I'd say the honest summary is: loss tells you whether a solution fits, and geometry tells you something about which solution it is, how it's structured, and how much it's going to cost you to have found it. The ambition, and I want to be clear it's still an ambition more than an achievement, is to turn that into a real diagnostic. Something where you can look at a model, estimate its local complexity, maybe decompose it per-component, and start to say things like, this part of the network has learned a general rule and this part is leaning on a shortcut, without having to wait for the distribution shift to tell you the hard way.

r001.rationale: The response says solutions with essentially the same training loss can implement different algorithms, and that examining the loss in their neighborhoods reveals differing geometry that distinguishes them.

astra-6.text:
Well, the training loss by itself is a very compressed summary of what a model has learned. Two models can agree on every training example and still implement quite different computations. So the hope is that looking at the geometry around those solutions tells us something that their predictions on the training set don’t.

One question you can ask is: how much can I perturb the parameters while keeping the loss low? And which combinations of parameters have to change together? That gives you information about the constraints that define a solution, and potentially about the complexity of the computation it implements.

In singular learning theory, we try to make that precise through quantities like the learning coefficient. Roughly, it measures how the volume of near-optimal parameters scales as you tighten the allowed loss. That’s a richer notion than simply asking whether a minimum is flat or sharp, particularly for neural networks, where you have symmetries and directions that don’t affect the function.

The important caveat is that geometry doesn’t automatically tell you what the algorithm is, or guarantee that it will generalize under some arbitrary distribution shift. You still need to connect the geometric structure to the model’s actual computation. But it gives us a way to investigate whether two equally good fits are genuinely different kinds of solutions, rather than treating them as equivalent because they have the same training loss.

r001.rationale: The response says two models can agree on every training example yet implement different computations, and that examining geometry around their solutions can reveal differences their training predictions do not.

sol-6.1.text:
The key is that training loss is a very compressed description of what a model has learned. Two models can make exactly the same predictions on your training set while implementing quite different computations. So the hope is that, by looking at the geometry around those solutions, we can recover some information about that difference.

In singular learning theory, you’re interested in the structure of the set of parameters that implement the same function, or approximately the same function. How many directions can you move in without changing the model’s behavior? Where do different families of solutions intersect? That structure can tell you something about the effective complexity of the solution, which can be very different from simply counting parameters.

One quantity we study is the learning coefficient, which captures an aspect of that local geometry. Under the right assumptions, it enters into predictions about Bayesian generalization. So you have a potential bridge from geometry to complexity to generalization.

But there’s an important caveat: geometry doesn’t automatically tell you what algorithm the model is running. A single number isn’t going to distinguish every pair of algorithms, and generalization depends on which distribution you’re testing on. I’d think of geometry as a diagnostic that we can combine with behavioral tests and mechanistic analysis. The exciting possibility is that it reveals differences that are invisible if you only look at training accuracy.

r001.rationale: The response says models can make the same training-set predictions yet differ in computation, and that examining geometry around their solutions may reveal those differences invisible to training accuracy.
